To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the social contact network of the Portland metropolitan area is well-modeled by an appropriate variant of a random graph model, (ii) the model is useful for understanding many key structural features of the network, and (iii) the model is also useful for designing fast approximation algorithms for important structural properties of the social contact networks.

(i) the social network of a city can be modeled by a bipartite random graph; (ii) the social network is well-modeled by the CL-model; (iii) the CL-model can be efficiently generated; (iv) the dominating set problem is well-approximable in such networks; (v) the social network has interesting structural properties such as the clustering coefficient, and the shortest path distribution

1) the CL-model is a good approximation to the Portland social contact network; 2) we can generate random networks with similar structural properties as the Portland social contact networks in near linear time; and 3) we have fast approximation algorithms for many basic structural properties of such networks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the structure of very large, very sparse, and very complex social networks, and developing algorithms that can exploit this structure.

the following questions: What can we learn from the structure of social contact networks? What is the best way to model these networks? What are efficient ways to compute and approximate basic structural properties? How can we efficiently generate large-scale social contact networks?

the algorithmic and statistical aspects of very large, very complex, and very realistic social contact networks, which are important in many applications, including the study of large-scale epidemics.

our results provide the first comprehensive study of the structure of a very large social contact network, with the first fast algorithms to compute key structural parameters, the first fast approximation algorithms to compute near-optimal sensor-placement, and the first fast methods to generate random graphs with the same key features.
our results show that the CL-model is a useful and expressive model of the social network, and that many basic structural properties can be computed efficiently for this model.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that many basic structural properties of large, realistic social-contact networks can be well-modeled and approximated in near-linear time.

we are able to provide fast approximation algorithms for many key structural and algorithmic properties of very large social contact networks, and we are able to generate random networks with similar structural properties.
, in addition to being of interest for their own sake, these social networks have many applications in the areas of epidemiology, transportation, and social science.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the social network is a crucial component of any model for studying epidemics, and it can be modeled as a bipartite random graph with a power law degree distribution.
the CL-model is an extremely useful model for generating large-scale, realistic social contact graphs, which are useful in a variety of applications, such as disease-detection and disease-control.
a random-graph approach can provide a good approximation to a very large social network.
